title: Java News Roundup: Simple JSON API, GlassFish, Jakarta EE, JNoSQL, Open Liberty, LangChain4j
gist: Weekly Java ecosystem roundup for August 10th 2026: JDK 28 gains a proposed-to-target Simple JSON API (JEP 540) that removes the need for external JSON libraries, and proposes deprecating the macOS/x64 port (JEP 541) because Apple no longer supports the architecture. Alongside, Jakarta EE 12 specs including a new Jakarta Agentic AI 1.0 hit milestones, Open Liberty 26.0.0.8 patches three denial-of-service CVEs, and LangChain4j 1.19.0 adds an Anthropic Message Batches API model class.

insights.claim: JEP 540, Simple JSON API (Incubator), has been elevated from Candidate to Proposed to Target for JDK 28, defining a standard API for parsing and generating JSON documents without an external library and implementing RFC 8259.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Absorbing JSON handling into the JDK erodes the default-dependency position of third-party libraries like Jackson and Gson across the Java ecosystem.

insights.claim: JEP 540 supersedes JEP 198, Light-Weight JSON API, which is now closed and withdrawn, showing OpenJDK restarted rather than revived its earlier attempt at built-in JSON support.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A decade-scale lag between first attempt and delivery is the realistic cadence for JDK standard-library expansion — temper expectations on other pending JEPs.

insights.claim: JEP 541 proposes deprecating the macOS/x64 port for removal in JDK 28 because Apple no longer supports that architecture, with the explicit intent of saving maintenance costs.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Confirms Intel-based Mac support is being retired from core developer toolchains, forcing hardware refresh cycles on teams still on x64 Macs.
insights.quote: This JEP proposes to deprecate the macOS/x64 port as Apple no longer supports this architecture.
insights.locator: JEP 541, Deprecate the macOS/x64 Port for Removal

insights.claim: The macOS/x64 deprecation follows the same playbook as JEP 449's deprecation of the Windows 32-bit x86 port, indicating OpenJDK now systematically prunes legacy architecture ports to control maintenance burden.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A repeatable pruning pattern lets you predict which platforms lose Java support next — relevant for long-lived embedded and enterprise estates.
insights.locator: Similar to JEP 449, Deprecate the Windows 32-bit x86 Port

insights.claim: JDK 27 early-access remains at Build 34 while JDK 28 early-access advanced to Build 11, with the JEP 541 review closing August 21, 2026 and the JEP 540 review closing August 17, 2026.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Concrete review deadlines mark when JDK 28's feature set locks — the checkpoint for planning migration work.
insights.locator: Build 34 remains the current build in the JDK 27 early-access builds

insights.claim: Jakarta EE 12 specifications are progressing unevenly: Jakarta CDI 5.0 is up for release review and JSON Binding 3.1 has an M2 shaping up, but Jakarta RESTful Web Services 5.0 is blocked waiting on three required +1 approvals to merge pull requests before it can produce an M1.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Committer review bandwidth, not engineering work, is the gating factor on Jakarta EE 12 timing — a governance risk for enterprise roadmaps pegged to it.
insights.quote: the team is waiting for the three required +1s to get the pull requests merged before they are able to produce an M1
insights.locator: In his weekly Hashtag Jakarta EE blog

insights.claim: The Jakarta Agentic AI 1.0 specification, approved for creation in early November 2025, has delivered an M1 release and launched a new project website.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Enterprise Java is formalising an agentic-AI standard roughly nine months after approval — a signal that agent frameworks are moving from vendor libraries toward committee specification.

insights.claim: GlassFish 9.0.0 milestone 3 delivers full implementations of Jakarta Security 5.0-M2, Jakarta Faces 5.0-M5 and CDI 5.0-RC1, only a partial Jakarta Servlet 6.2-M2, and no implementation yet of Jakarta Concurrency 3.2-M3.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The reference implementation trailing the specs on Servlet and Concurrency is the practical gate on when Jakarta EE 12 becomes deployable.
insights.locator: The third milestone release of GlassFish 9.0.0

insights.claim: GlassFish 9.0.0-M3 adds first-class support for applying the Jakarta Annotations @RolesAllowed annotation in Jakarta RESTful Web Services endpoints integrated with Jakarta Security, extended to include template paths.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Declarative role security reaching REST template paths closes a long-standing gap that forced custom authorization filters in enterprise Java apps.
insights.locator: This release also features initial first-class support

insights.claim: Open Liberty 26.0.0.8 GA resolves multiple CVEs that can all result in denial-of-service, and developers are explicitly encouraged to upgrade.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A clustered DoS-CVE release is an operational forcing event for enterprises running Liberty in production.
insights.locator: The GA release of Open Liberty 26.0.0.8

insights.claim: CVE-2026-50645 stems from Apache CXF placing no restrictions on the number of attachment headers a message can contain during deserialization, enabling uncontrolled resource consumption in Jakarta RESTful Web Services implementations.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: The vulnerability sits in a widely embedded upstream component, so exposure extends beyond Open Liberty to any stack shipping Apache CXF.

insights.claim: Two further Open Liberty flaws, CVE-2026-9171 and CVE-2026-15057, allow attackers to force unnecessary memory consumption via specially-crafted requests and uncontrolled heap allocation respectively.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Three memory-exhaustion CVEs in one release points to unbounded-allocation as the recurring class of flaw in Java application servers.

themes.theme: Java AI tooling and data connectors

insights.claim: LangChain4j 1.19.0 ships a new AnthropicBatchChatModel class implementing the Anthropic Message Batches API, bringing batch LLM inference into the mainstream Java AI framework.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Batch APIs are the cheapest per-token inference tier; first-class Java support widens the enterprise workloads that can economically move to LLMs.
insights.locator: The formal release (along with the twenty-ninth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.19.0

insights.claim: LangChain4j 1.19.0 adds functionality to map a _meta object from an MCP server within the attributes() method of ToolExecutionResult, treating MCP metadata as a first-class application data channel.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: MCP plumbing landing inside stable Java framework APIs is evidence the protocol is consolidating as the tool-calling standard.
insights.locator: new functionality to map a _meta object from an MCP server

insights.claim: Eclipse JNoSQL 1.1.16 adds support for Valkey, the open source key/value datastore, alongside improved Oracle NoSQL integration and driver updates for MongoDB, DynamoDB, Couchbase, OrientDB and Elasticsearch.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Valkey entering a Jakarta NoSQL implementation marks the Redis fork reaching enterprise-standard status — a competitive datapoint for Redis Inc.

themes.theme: Native image and JVM language tooling

insights.claim: GraalVM Native Build Tools 1.1.9 elevates Native Image layers from an experimental, binary-scoped Gradle feature into a shared model with first-class Gradle and Maven support.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Layered native images cut build times and image size, removing a key friction point for Java in serverless and container-dense deployments.
insights.locator: The release of GraalVM Native Build Tools 1.1.9

insights.claim: Apache Groovy 6.0.0 beta 2 adopts JEP 371 Hidden Classes, delivered back in JDK 15, for the many short-lived synthetic classes Groovy generates at runtime.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A roughly six-year lag between a JDK feature shipping and a major JVM language consuming it shows how slowly platform improvements propagate into the ecosystem.
insights.locator: The second beta release of Apache Groovy 6.0.0

insights.claim: Groovy 6.0.0 beta 2 introduces a GeneratedDispatcher interface specifically so that Packed Closures work when generating native images, indicating native-image compatibility is now a design constraint on dynamic JVM languages.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Ahead-of-time compilation is reshaping dynamic-language design in the JVM, a structural tailwind for GraalVM-style deployment.
insights.locator: a new GeneratedDispatcher interface so that Packed Closures work
